newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Historic square focus of Albanian investor protest.
newsitem.headline: Historic square focus of Albanian investor protest.

text.p: In the square where Albania declared independence more than 80 years ago, thousands of people now gather to demand a different type of country.
"We want a new government, a new democracy," Kastriot, 42, said on Thursday, the second consecutive day of protests in the Adriatic port of Vlore. "Most of all, we want our money back."

The explosion of anger in the normally peaceful run-down town was triggered by the collapse of the local Gjallica pyramid scheme, which owed depositors $500 million. Most people blame Albania's right-wing government for the calamity.
"They've stolen our money. This government is nothing better than a bunch of lying thieves," said, Merita, accompanied at a night-time street procession by two toddlers.

President Sali Berisha, founder of the ruling Democratic Party, has denied any government involvement in the failure of a string of popular pyramid investment schemes and says the government cannot afford refunds for everyone.
"We will march until we get our money. We will march to Tirana," Merita said. Her 3 1/2-year-old son endlessly repeated the chant: "Sali, you thief, where have you put our money?"
The rallies are disorganised, spontaneous and chaotic. There are no opposition party leaders at the head of a column, no rabble-rousing speakers addressing the throng.
"We dont need politicians. We voted for Berisha and look what happened to us," said one elderly man. "We just need our money and food to eat."
The police tried to disperse the crowd on the first day of protests but eventually gave way. Now the marchers passed unhindered, although some fear a future crackdown.

"The police have threatened us with arrest. Maybe not now, but next week or the week after that," said Ilir, in his late twenties. "But I have no choice. I've lost all money, I'm living in a tent. Better prison than a tent."
Demonstrators held candles aloft to show the way down the darkened boulevard.
Younger marchers paused to hurl stones at the unfinished concrete "business centre" which was supposed to house the now-ruined Gjallica scheme and an advertising hoarding displaying its dove symbol.
Without warning, a white sports car charged down the road scattering hundreds of terrified people.
"Drunk hooligan," muttered a policeman. Demonstrators said it was an undercover agent trying to provoke violence.
"We are not going to fight them. We're peaceful here," one man said.
But others said that unless refunds were forthcoming soon, collective patience would snap and the city would explode.
"The politicians have vanished," said a young woman. "If they don't come and explain the situation soon and give us back our cash, we'll get violent."

When the marchers reached Vlore's port, they turned heel and walked back over the rutted road to Independence Square where Albania was declared a state in November 1912 after more than four centuries of Turkish rule.
"They hoisted the national flag here," said one elderly woman wrapped up against the winter chill. "We should now lower it to half-mast to mourn this disaster."
